title: The Bill at Dawn

post.author: u/night_books_drusilla
post.title: I do the night books for a wine merchant. At 06:00 the provider's email said one night of tasting notes cost $2,648.47. The note for bottle 5,812 calls it softer than the Riesling we opened earlier. Nobody opened anything.

blocks.text: I'm Drusilla, the night bookkeeper at Ferrabee's, a wine merchant on the high street. When the shop shuts I do the books: the day's takings, the stock, the bills.

Every new bottle in the stock book gets a tasting note, a few lines on how it smells and tastes. A language model writes them: a program that reads text and writes text back. A company called a provider runs it and bills us for the text, both ways.

It counts text in tokens, small pieces of words, like tiles in a word game. Our price list: $3 for every million tokens we send it, and $15 for every million it writes. Writing costs five times as much as reading. The provider's small model costs a tenth: 30 cents and $1.50.
At midnight a job starts: a small program that Mr Lightowler, our part-time developer, wrote and runs on a rented computer.

Until October it sent one request per bottle: one message carrying our standing instructions (1,500 tokens) and that bottle's details (300), and one note of about 200 tokens back. Forty bottles, a normal night, cost 34 cents.

On 1 October he rewrote it so the notes would sound like one voice. Now each night is one conversation, and each bottle is a turn in it. The model remembers nothing between requests. So every request sends the whole conversation again: the instructions, every earlier bottle and note, then the new bottle. Each turn adds about 500 tokens. Bottle 40 sends 21,300. Forty bottles came to 462,000 tokens, $1.51 a night. Nobody noticed 34 cents become $1.51.

His code keeps each request at or under 150,000 tokens. When one would pass that, it drops the oldest turns first; that is called trimming. From bottle 298, every request carries the instructions and the last 296 bottles: 149,800 tokens, about three and a half seconds each.

Yesterday afternoon Mrs Ferrabee bought the whole cellar of the Kittering estate. Its list went into the stock book as 6,000 new bottles, numbered 1 to 6,000. I spent the night downstairs, checking crates against that list. The shop computer is upstairs.
At 06:00 I came up to the provider's daily email. Each line shows what it counted in the 24 hours before.

Ferrabee's   usage, 24 hours to 06:00, 15 October
requests     6,000
tokens sent  876,822,000
tokens back  1,200,000
spend        $2,648.47
day before   $1.51

Then I read the notes. Bottle 5,812, a 1985 claret, written at 05:31: "Softer than the Riesling we opened earlier, and more patient." Bottle 5,790 is a 2017 Riesling from the estate. It is in crate 193, its wax unbroken. I checked.
Nobody opened anything. Something upstairs tasted six thousand bottles anyway.

From bottle 298, at 00:09:58, every request carried 149,800 tokens, until the last note at 05:42:16.

blocks.text: Mr Lightowler says nothing looped: 6,000 bottles, 6,000 requests, each done once. Mrs Ferrabee says she'd gladly pay $40 to have an estate written up, and never $2,648.47. The next estate sale is in November. What should we change?

comments.author: u/gradient_ghost
comments.text: Nothing in your cellar was opened, though patient is a fair word for a 1985 claret. The model keeps nothing between requests; the conversation exists only in what your job sends it each time. Two words you'll meet on the billing page. A spend alert is an email the provider sends once your spending passes a line you choose. A budget is a limit on what one job may spend, checked before each request, so the job stops instead of carrying on. Three questions. Of the $2,648.47, how much paid for the writing? Which bottles did the request for 5,812 carry? And has a note ever mentioned another bottle before tonight?

replies.author: u/night_books_drusilla
replies.text: The writing was $18.00 of it: 1,200,000 tokens back. The request for 5,812 carried 149,800 tokens: the instructions and bottles 5,516 to 5,811, the Riesling among them. I searched October's notes. Three, on quiet nights, mention another bottle opened earlier; each time it was earlier the same night, in the same conversation. Nobody had read them that closely. Mr Lightowler showed me the billing page too. It also offers a batch: you hand over a pile of separate requests at once and collect the answers later, at half price. The page says most finish within an hour.

comments.author: u/small_model_cradock
comments.text: The model is the expensive part. Your own price list says the small one charges a tenth for every token, reading and writing. Switch the job to it and the bill shrinks tenfold, same code, nothing to rewrite. A tasting note isn't hard work; right now you're paying a sommelier, a trained wine waiter, to read labels.

replies.author: u/night_books_drusilla
replies.text: Mr Lightowler likes this. He says it's one line in the settings.

comments.author: u/fifty_words_ailbhe
comments.text: Writing costs five times reading, so the notes are where the money goes. Yours run about 150 words. Cap them at fifty and every answer costs about a third as much. Nobody reads past the first line of a tasting note anyway.

reply.prompt: The next estate sale is in November. What should Ferrabee's change before then? Part 2 follows your advice.

options.text: Move the tasting-note job to a cheaper model that charges a tenth as much for each token.
options.verdict: A tenth of the wrong shape
options.part2: Mr Lightowler moved the job to the small model, and we replayed the estate's night in the sim. The same conversation sent the same 6,000 requests and the same 876,822,000 tokens. The bill came to $264.85: a tenth, and still 175 times a normal night's $1.51. Bottle 5,812's request still carried bottles 5,516 to 5,811, the Riesling among them. And nothing would stop the job on a bigger estate.
options.senior: Price per token is one lever; tokens per request is the other, and here it was the bigger one. One request per bottle sends 1,800 tokens; tonight's conversation averaged about 146,000 a request (876,822,000 / 6,000). On any price list, that shape reads about 81 times as much: $2,630.47 against $32.40. Route plain work to a cheaper model after the shape is right: one request per bottle on the small model, batched, writes the whole estate for $2.52, if a sample of its notes reads well. And read the small print: on Anthropic's pricing page, one small model charges more once a request's prompt passes 100,000 tokens, so a long history can lose the very discount you switched for.

options.text: Send each bottle as its own request, batched overnight, with a job budget that stops it.
options.part2: Mr Lightowler put back one request per bottle: our instructions, with a few example notes for the house voice, and that one bottle. That is 1,800 tokens sent and about 200 back, $0.0084 a bottle, $50.40 for the estate. Each request stands alone, so they can go in a batch: at midnight the job hands the provider all 6,000 and collects the answers later, at half price. The estate's night replays at $25.20, and the provider says most batches finish within an hour, long before I come up at 06:00. Over the job he set a budget of $40 a night, checked before every request. With this shape it is never reached. When we played the old conversation under it, the job stopped after bottle 225, at $39.69, at 00:06:12. Bottle 5,812's request held only bottle 5,812, and its note mentions no other wine.
options.senior: Work out cost per request before you ship: tokens sent times the reading price, plus tokens written times the writing price. Then multiply by the most requests one night can bring, a whole estate included. A conversation is the wrong shape for items that don't need each other: the model is stateless, so every turn sends the history again, and request k costs about k times the first until a trim caps it at its most expensive. Give each item only what it needs, and keep the house voice in the standing instructions. Work that can wait goes in a batch: Anthropic's batch page says all usage is charged at 50% of standard prices and most batches finish within an hour, with a 24-hour limit. Put a budget on the job that stops it, sized from its biggest honest night (6,000 bottles batched is $25.20, so $40 leaves room), and keep an alert below it as a second line. Then route plain notes to the small model if a sample reads well.

options.text: Cap every tasting note at fifty words, so each answer the model writes costs far less.
options.verdict: The writing was never the bill
options.part2: Mr Lightowler capped the notes at fifty words, about 65 tokens. We replayed the night. The tokens written fell from 1,200,000 to 390,000, and the writing from $18.00 to $5.85. The night came to $2,615.20, $33.27 less. Shorter notes made each turn smaller, so the history held 406 bottles instead of 296, and every request from bottle 407 on still carried 149,990 tokens. Bottle 5,812's request held bottles 5,406 to 5,811, the Riesling still among them.
options.senior: Find where the money goes before you cut. Writing costs five times reading per token, so trimming the answers is tempting. But tonight the model read 876,822,000 tokens and wrote 1,200,000: the writing was $18.00 of $2,648.47, 0.68%. In the one-per-bottle shape the writing is 35.71% of the bill and worth watching; in a growing conversation the history drowns it. Shorter answers also make each turn smaller, so a trimmed history simply holds more turns. Read the tokens in and out that the provider reports with every answer, per request, before choosing a lever.

options.text: Set a spend alert that emails the bookkeeper as soon as a night passes fifty dollars.
options.part2: Mr Lightowler set a spend alert at $50. We replayed the night: it fired at 00:07:37, after bottle 254, at $50.33. The email went to the shop computer upstairs, and I was downstairs with the crates until 06:00. Had I read it, I couldn't have stopped a job on his rented computer, and he was asleep. The night still cost $2,648.47.
options.senior: An alert is worth having: it is cheap, and it catches what nobody planned for. But it tells a person, and the spending between the email and someone acting has no limit: here, a sleeping developer and a bookkeeper in the cellar. A budget acts with nobody awake. Use both: a budget that stops each job, sized from its biggest honest night, and an alert below it that says a job is heading there. A provider's account-wide spend limit (a6e01) is a last fence, and it stops every tool at once; a per-job budget usually lives in your own code or a gateway.

sim.title: Replay the estate's night in a cost ledger
sim.lede: You're Drusilla, replaying the night of 14 to 15 October from midnight, with nothing sent yet. No real model runs here: every number comes from one price list and stated token counts. The standing instructions are 1,500 tokens, each bottle's details 300, each note about 200 (about 65 if capped at fifty words). In one conversation each request also carries every earlier turn, and the code drops the oldest turns to stay at or under 150,000 tokens. Prices: $3 per million tokens sent and $15 per million written; the small model a tenth, $0.30 and $1.50; a batch half price, for separate requests only. The job starts at 00:00:00 and sends requests one after another; each takes 0.5 seconds plus 1 second per 50,000 tokens sent. A budget is checked before each request; an alert emails once spending passes its line.
sim.tryThis: Try this: press Run the night and read $2,648.47, trimming from bottle 298, and bottle 5,812's request holding bottles 5,516 to 5,811, its note done at 05:31:19. Set 40 bottles for a normal night: $1.51. Switch to one request per bottle, go back to 6,000 and read $50.40; turn on the batch: $25.20. Put the $40 budget on the conversation and watch it stop after bottle 225. Then play each reply.

explain.oneLine: Nothing tasted the Riesling. Since 1 October the note job ran each night as one conversation, and because the model remembers nothing, every request sent every earlier bottle again. On a 40-bottle night that cost $1.51; on the estate's 6,000 it sent 876,822,000 tokens, and note 5,812 was written with the Riesling's note still in its history.

steps.title: What one request costs.
steps.text: A request's bill is worked out in steps. First count every token it sends: here the instructions and the bottle's details, 1,800. Second multiply by the reading price: 1,800 x $3 / 1,000,000 = $0.0054. Third count the tokens written and multiply by the writing price: 200 x $15 / 1,000,000 = $0.003. Last add them: $0.0084 a bottle, 34 cents for 40. On the provider's pricing page writing costs five times reading on every row, so per token the answer is dearer; per request, what you send is often the bigger part. What can go wrong: an estimate that counts only the new text, not everything the request carries.

steps.title: Why a conversation costs more every turn.
steps.text: The model keeps nothing between requests. Anthropic's page puts it plainly: the Messages API is stateless, which means that you always send the full conversational history. So a conversation runs in steps. First the job sends the instructions and bottle 1. Second it adds note 1 and bottle 2, and sends all of it. Third it adds note 2 and bottle 3, and sends all of that, each turn 500 tokens longer. Request k carries 1,800 + 500 x (k - 1) tokens, so the total grows with the square of the bottles: 40 bottles send 72,000 + 390,000 = 462,000 tokens, more than six times the 72,000 of one request each, and 6,000 with no trim would send about 9 billion. What can go wrong: each turn looks cheap, and nobody adds up the night.

steps.title: The trim, and the estate's night.
steps.text: Mr Lightowler's code keeps each request at or under 150,000 tokens. In steps: first it builds the request; second, if it would pass 150,000, it drops the oldest turn, and again, until it fits; third it sends what is left. From bottle 298 every request carries the instructions and the last 296 bottles, 149,800 tokens, about 3.5 seconds each. So 6,000 bottles sent 297 growing requests (22,512,600 tokens) and 5,703 full ones (854,309,400): 876,822,000 tokens, $2,630.47, plus $18.00 of writing, $2,648.47. Note 5,812, done at 05:31:19, was written beside bottles 5,516 to 5,811. The 2017 Riesling, 5,790, was 22 bottles back, and a model asked for a tasting note compared the two as if both were open. What can go wrong: a trim caps each request's size, not their number, and holds every later request at its most expensive.

steps.title: Why the quick fixes miss.
steps.text: The small model at a tenth: the same 876,822,000 tokens, $264.85, 175 times a normal night. Fifty-word notes: the writing falls from $18.00 to $5.85, the night only to $2,615.20, because reading was 99.32% of the bill. A spend alert at $50 fires at 00:07:37, after bottle 254, to a computer nobody reads until 06:00, and stops nothing. Each pulls a lever that matters somewhere; none changes how many tokens each bottle sends. This was not a4e08's runaway loop: there were 6,000 bottles and 6,000 requests, each made once. What can go wrong: fixing the price of a token while the count of tokens is the bill.

steps.title: The right shape: one request each, a batch, a budget.
steps.text: One request per bottle carries 1,800 tokens: 6,000 bottles send 10,800,000 and get 1,200,000 back, $50.40, done by 00:53:36 one after another. Each request stands alone, so they can go in a batch, which runs in steps: first the job hands over all 6,000 at once; second the provider answers each on its own when it has room; third the job collects the results. Anthropic's batch page says all usage is charged at 50% of standard prices and most batches finish within an hour: $25.20. A conversation can't be batched, because each turn needs the answer before it. Then the budget: before each request the job adds its cost to the night's spending and stops if that would pass $40. Under it the old conversation stops after bottle 225, at $39.69, at 00:06:12. Routing plain notes to the small model takes the estate to $2.52, if a sample reads well. Build Night X5 builds budgets and routing into a gateway. What can go wrong: a budget set too tight stops honest nights; size it from the biggest one.

diagram.aria: The fix. The stock book's 6,000 new bottles go to the note job, which builds one request per bottle and checks a $40 budget before each. It hands all 6,000 at once to the batch, at half price, which passes them to the provider's model, $3 and $15 a million, and most batches come back within an hour. To the right, greyed out, the old shape: one conversation, $2,648.47 a night.

explain.caption: Read from the top left. The stock book's 6,000 new bottles go to the note job, which builds one request per bottle, 1,800 tokens each, and checks the $40 budget before each one. It hands all 6,000 to the batch at once, at half price; the provider's model answers each on its own, and most batches come back within an hour: $25.20 for the estate. The old shape, one conversation at $2,648.47, is greyed out on the right.

fix.title: The fix: one request per bottle, in a batch, under a budget that stops the job
fix.text: Send each bottle as its own request, with only what that bottle needs: the standing instructions, a few example notes for the house voice, and its details, 1,800 tokens. Because nobody needs the notes before morning, hand the night's requests over as one batch at half price, and collect them when it finishes. Put a budget on the job, checked before every request, that stops it at $40 a night: the estate's 6,000 bottles fit at $25.20, and any shape that sends far more stops within minutes. Keep a spend alert below it for the person who reads the books. Then try the small model on a sample of notes, and route plain descriptions to it if they read well: $2.52 for the estate. Log each request's tokens in and out, so the next change to the job shows up in the numbers the first night.

limits: A batch trades speed for price. Most finish within an hour, but Anthropic's page allows up to 24 hours and says batches can expire; a note needed by opening time needs a plan for the ones that don't come back.

A budget stops the spending and the work. When it trips, some bottles have no note until someone looks, so the job must say which ones, and the budget must be sized from the biggest honest night, or it will stop the next estate sale.

One request per bottle loses the shared voice the conversation was for, and each note sees no other bottle. Keep the house style and a few example notes in the standing instructions, and read a sample after any change.

explain.seniorTake: Estimate the cost per request of a feature built on an LLM, a large language model, before you ship it: tokens sent times the reading price plus tokens written times the writing price, then times the most requests one run can bring. Writing usually costs several times reading per token, but what you send is often most of the bill, because instructions, documents and history ride along with every request. A model is stateless, so a conversation sends its whole history every turn and costs more each time; use one only when the turns really need each other, and give independent items one request each with only what they need. Put work that can wait in a batch at half price. Give every job its own budget that stops it, sized from its biggest honest run, with an alert below it, because an alert alone only tells someone. Route plain work to a cheaper model once the shape is right and a sample passes. Then log tokens in and out per request, so a change in shape shows on the first night, not the first bill.

realWorld.title: Anthropic pricing: writing costs five times reading
realWorld.text: Anthropic's pricing page lists a base input price and an output price per million tokens for each model, and on every row the output price is five times the input price, for example $3 / MTok in and $15 / MTok out. It defines MTok: Million tokens. $5 / MTok is $5 for every million tokens. This case's price list uses the same ratio and names no model.

realWorld.title: Anthropic pricing: a long request costs per token like a short one
realWorld.text: The same page says that for its larger models a 900k-token request is billed at the same per-token rate as a 9k-token request. A long history is never discounted; you pay for every token of it, every time. And one small model on the page is priced by prompt length: a request whose prompt is over 100,000 tokens pays higher prices.

realWorld.title: Anthropic batch processing: half price, most within an hour
realWorld.text: The Message Batches API page says all usage is charged at 50% of the standard API prices, and that the system processes each batch as fast as possible, with most batches completing within 1 hour. Batches expire if processing does not complete within 24 hours. A batch is limited to either 100,000 Message requests or 256 MB in size, whichever is reached first.

realWorld.title: Batch requests are handled independently
realWorld.text: The page says the batch is processed asynchronously, with each request handled independently, and that the approach is well-suited to tasks that do not require immediate responses. That is why one request per bottle can go in a batch and one conversation cannot: each turn needs the answer before it.

realWorld.title: Anthropic Messages API: stateless
realWorld.text: Anthropic's guide to the Messages API says: The Messages API is stateless, which means that you always send the full conversational history to the API. Every turn of a conversation is a new request that carries all the turns before it.

asked: How do you estimate the cost of an LLM feature?
Why does a chat cost more per turn?
When would you use a batch interface?
interview.answer: I work it out per request first. Tokens sent times the input price, plus tokens written times the output price; output is usually several times dearer per token, but input is often most of the bill, because instructions, retrieved documents and history ride along every time. Then I multiply by the requests a busy run can bring, not an average day: here 1,800 tokens in and 200 out is $0.0084 a bottle, and an estate sale is 6,000 bottles. A chat costs more per turn because the API is stateless: every request re-sends the whole conversation, so turn k carries about k turns, and the total grows with the square of the turns until a trim caps each request at its most expensive. So I use a conversation only when the turns need each other, and send independent items as separate requests with only what they need. I use a batch interface for work nobody is waiting on, like overnight descriptions or evals: about half price, results usually within an hour, but up to a day, so I plan for late or expired items. Every job gets its own budget that stops it, sized from its biggest honest run, with an alert below it, and I route plain work to a cheaper model once a sample passes. Finally I log tokens in and out per request, so a change in shape shows on the first night.

atWork: Look for an overnight job that sends a growing history with every call. It is a common pattern: a script rewritten as one chat conversation so its outputs sound consistent, a summariser that keeps every earlier summary in the request, an agent that never drops its notes. Each request looks cheap on a quiet night, and the bill only moves when a run is suddenly large. Ask four things. What does one request cost, in tokens sent and written, and what does the biggest honest run multiply it by? Does each request carry anything the item doesn't need? Is any of this work waiting on nobody, and could it go in a batch at half price? And what stops a job that suddenly spends a hundred times its normal night: its own budget, or an email someone reads in the morning? If the answers point at a gateway with budgets and routing per job, Build Night X5 is where you build one. Standards-readiness note: if your organisation is certified to ISO/IEC 27001:2022 or working toward it, Annex A control A.8.6 (capacity management) expects the use of resources to be monitored and adjusted against current and expected needs, which per-job token budgets and logged tokens per request support. If you hold ISO 9001:2015, clause 9.1 asks you to monitor and measure your processes, and what a process costs per run is one of those measures. Building a budget and a token log into the job from its first version is far cheaper than explaining a dawn bill to an auditor.

recall.prompt: Your support team's assistant summarises each closed ticket overnight. To keep the summaries consistent, a developer runs the night's 2,000 tickets through one chat conversation, trimmed at 100,000 tokens. The bill has jumped from $4 to $500 a night, and nothing is looping. What is happening, and what would you change?

keyIdeas.idea: Every request re-sends the whole conversation so far, so each ticket costs more than the last
Send each ticket as its own request carrying only what it needs
Nobody needs it before morning: send it as a batch at about half the price

recall.model: The model is stateless, so in one conversation every request re-sends the whole history: the instructions plus every earlier ticket and summary. Each ticket costs more than the last until the trim holds every request near 100,000 tokens, and then each one is as expensive as it can be. Nothing loops; the shape is the bill. Send each ticket as its own request, with the instructions and a couple of example summaries for consistency, and only that ticket. Nobody needs the summaries before morning, so hand them over as a batch at half price; most batches finish within an hour. Then put a budget on the job that stops it, sized from the busiest honest night, and log tokens in and out per request.

recall.prompt: A request sends 20,000 tokens and gets 500 back. The price list is $3 per million tokens sent and $15 per million written. What does the request cost?
recall.why: Reading: 20,000 x $3 / 1,000,000 = $0.06. Writing: 500 x $15 / 1,000,000 = $0.0075. Together $0.0675. $0.0600 forgets the writing; $0.3015 swaps the two prices. Even at five times the price per token, the writing is only a ninth of this bill.

recall.prompt: A team plans to put 40,000 product descriptions through a model overnight, one request each, and nobody needs them before morning. Someone proposes an email at $100 as the only protection. What would you add, and why?

keyIdeas.idea: The work can wait, so send it as a batch: about half the price, usually back within an hour
A budget on the job that stops it, not only a message that tells someone
An email needs someone awake and able to act; the spending in between has no limit

recall.model: An email at $100 is worth keeping, but it only tells someone, and overnight that someone is usually asleep, so the spending after it has no limit. Add a budget on the job that stops it before each request once the night's spending would pass a line, sized from the biggest honest run. Work out the cost per request first, tokens sent and written times their prices, and multiply by 40,000 so the budget leaves room. And because nobody needs the descriptions before morning, send them as a batch at half price; most batches finish within an hour, but plan for the few that take longer.

recall.prompt: In Ferrabee's conversation, bottle k's request sends 1,800 + 500 x (k - 1) tokens. With no trim, how many tokens do the first 40 bottles send in all?
recall.why: Forty requests of 1,800 make 72,000, plus 500 x (0 + 1 + ... + 39) = 500 x 780 = 390,000 for the history: 462,000. 21,300 is bottle 40's request alone. Sent one request each, the same 40 bottles would send only 72,000.

recall.prompt: On the estate's night the model read 876,822,000 tokens and wrote 1,200,000, at $3 and $15 per million. About what share of the $2,648.47 was the writing?
options: About five sixths, since writing costs five times as much
recall.why: Writing: 1,200,000 x $15 / 1,000,000 = $18.00, which is 0.68% of $2,648.47. Reading 876,822,000 tokens cost $2,630.47. Five times the price per token means little when the model reads over 700 tokens for every one it writes.

coldCase.update: UPDATE, 3 months later. The tasting notes now go one request per bottle, collected in the morning, under a $40 budget, and a December estate of 9,000 bottles cost $37.80. In January Mr Lightowler added a second job on the same $40 budget: for each new bottle it sends the model that bottle plus the details and notes of the 20 most alike in stock, about 11,800 tokens, and asks for suggested alternatives. On 14 January there were 1,500 new bottles. The new job ran first, sent request by request at full price, and spent $39.98 by bottle 1,062. The budget stopped both jobs. In the morning no new bottle had a tasting note.
coldCase.prompt: Reply to OP. What went wrong, and what should change?

keyIdeas.idea: Each job needs its own budget, so one job can't use up another's
Work out the new job's cost per request before shipping: about four and a half times a tasting note's
The new job can wait too: batch it at half price

coldCase.model: The budget did its job; it was shared by two jobs, so the new one used it up and starved the notes. Give each job its own budget, sized from its biggest honest night, and decide which runs first. Work out the new job's cost per request before shipping it: 11,800 tokens sent and about 150 written is $0.0354 + $0.00225, about $0.0377, roughly four and a half times a tasting note's $0.0084, so 1,500 bottles cost about $56 at full price, more than the whole $40. Nobody needs suggestions before morning either, so batch it at half price, about $28, and ask whether 20 neighbours each with full notes are needed or a short list of names would do.
